items.title: A retract induces an injection on fundamental groups, and a deformation retract induces an isomorphism
items.strategy: Let i:A→X be the inclusion and r:X→A a retraction. Functoriality turns r∘i=id_A into r_*∘i_*=id, so i_* is injective. For a deformation retract, the pointwise-fixed homotopy from id_X to i∘r is based at every point of A, so based-homotopy invariance gives i_*∘r_*=id as well. Keep the basepoint in A explicit in both clauses.

items.title: There is no retraction of the closed disk onto the unit circle
items.strategy: The closed disk is a nonempty convex subset of R^2 and therefore has a one-element fundamental group at the chosen unit-circle basepoint. The unit circle has fundamental group isomorphic to Z and is nontrivial. A retraction would make the inclusion-induced homomorphism injective by the preceding proposition, which is impossible for a homomorphism from a nontrivial group to the one-element group.

items.title: A fixed-point-free self-map of the disk produces a continuous retraction onto the unit circle
items.strategy: For a continuous f:D^2→D^2 with f(x)≠x, put v(x)=x-f(x) and let r(x)=f(x)+λ(x)v(x), where λ(x) is the larger solution of |f(x)+tv(x)|^2=1. Write the quadratic-formula expression explicitly. Its denominator |v(x)|^2 never vanishes, its radicand is nonnegative, and continuity follows componentwise from continuity of inner products, norms, quotients on their cozero sets, and the nonnegative square root. Convexity of the disk shows λ(x)≥1; uniqueness of the outward ray intersection gives r(x)=x on the boundary. Check separately that the formula remains valid when f(x) lies on the boundary and when f(x)=0.

items.title: Brouwer fixed-point theorem for the closed disk
items.strategy: Assume a continuous self-map of D^2 has no fixed point. The preceding formula then gives a continuous retraction D^2→S^1, contradicting the no-retraction theorem. The conclusion is existence only; no uniqueness claim is made.

items.title: A root-free complex polynomial gives nullhomotopic normalized circle loops
items.strategy: Let p be a complex polynomial with no zero. For R≥0, normalize p(Rh([t]))/p(R), where h:R/Z→S^1 is the published circle homeomorphism, and transport the value back to R/Z. The quotient is based at [0] and never vanishes. Varying R continuously down to zero gives a based homotopy to the constant loop. Establish continuity of polynomial evaluation and normalization componentwise from finite real polynomial algebra, and check R=0 explicitly rather than dividing by R.

items.title: The normalized large-radius loop of a monic degree-$n$ polynomial has degree $n$
items.strategy: Write p(z)=z^n+a_1z^{n-1}+...+a_n with n≥1 and choose R>max(1,|a_1|+...+|a_n|). On |z|=R the leading term strictly dominates the lower terms. Scaling all lower coefficients by s∈[0,1] therefore gives a zero-free based homotopy from the normalized p-loop to the standard n-fold circle loop. Degree invariance and the published degree of the standard loop give n. Check a vanishing lower-coefficient sum, n=1, and the strict inequality at every homotopy parameter.

items.title: Fundamental theorem of algebra by the fundamental-group obstruction
items.strategy: Assume a nonconstant complex polynomial has no root and divide by its leading coefficient to make it monic without changing its zero set. The root-free-loop lemma makes every normalized radius-R loop nullhomotopic and hence degree zero. At a radius satisfying the leading-term bound, the large-radius lemma gives degree n, where n≥1, a contradiction. Treat degree one and a zero constant coefficient within the same argument; the zero polynomial is excluded because it is not nonconstant.

items.title: The fundamental-group and minimum-modulus proofs of the fundamental theorem of algebra
An antipodal circle map has odd lift increment and is not nullhomotopic
items.strategy: Use S^1=R/Z and define its antipodal involution by a([u])=[u+1/2]. Let h satisfy h∘a=a∘h, and lift h∘p to a real path. If its value at 1/2 differs from its value at zero by k+1/2, uniqueness of path lifts on the first half interval forces the same relation on the second half. The total increment is 2k+1, so the loop cannot be endpoint-homotopic to a constant loop because homotopic lifts with a common initial value have the same endpoint. Prove a is well defined, and allow k to be negative; oddness, not positivity, is the point.

items.title: Borsuk–Ulam theorem in dimension two
items.strategy: If a continuous f:S^2→R^2 separates every antipodal pair, normalize f(x)-f(-x) to obtain a continuous odd map g:S^2→S^1. Restriction to the equator is non-nullhomotopic by the odd-lift lemma. But the equator loop is nullhomotopic in the simply connected S^2, and postcomposition by g preserves that nullhomotopy, a contradiction. Verify that the normalized difference never vanishes under the contrary hypothesis and that the equator parametrization respects antipodes.

items.title: There is no continuous injection from $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Borsuk–Ulam supplies x with f(x)=f(-x). On S^2 the equality x=-x would force x=0, contrary to unit norm, so x and -x are distinct and f is not injective.

items.title: One member of every three-set closed cover of $S^2$ contains an antipodal pair
items.strategy: For closed A_1,A_2,A_3 covering S^2, apply Borsuk–Ulam to the two distance functions d(-,A_1),d(-,A_2). Handle an empty A_i by replacing its undefined distance with the constant one function. Equality at an antipodal pair puts both points in A_1 or A_2 when the corresponding distance is zero; if both distances are positive, both points lie in A_3. Use closedness to identify zero distance with membership and treat all empty-set patterns explicitly.

items.title: Pointwise multiplication and concatenation of loops in a topological group agree up to homotopy
items.strategy: For based loops α and β at the identity, form the square (s,t)↦α(s)β(t). Traverse its boundary in the two coordinate orders and use explicit edge-preserving reparametrizations of the square to obtain endpoint-fixed homotopies between the pointwise product loop and each corresponding concatenation product. Continuity comes from the product universal property and continuous group multiplication. Fix the library's first-then-second concatenation convention when stating the order.

items.title: The fundamental group of a topological group is abelian
items.strategy: Loop concatenation and pointwise multiplication descend to two unital operations on loop classes. The preceding homotopies identify them, while the pointwise operation satisfies the interchange law. The Eckmann–Hilton calculation then gives [α][β]=[β][α]. Write the short calculation explicitly and check constant loops supply the common unit.

items.title: The punctured plane has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$, while punctured $\mathbb R^n$ is simply connected for $n\ge3$
items.strategy: At the standard basepoint e_0, radial deformation retraction identifies the punctured R^n fundamental group with that of S^{n-1}. For n=2 the geometric circle calculation gives Z. For n≥3, the sphere S^{n-1} is simply connected, so the group at every sphere basepoint is trivial. Join an arbitrary punctured-space basepoint x to x/|x| by its radial segment and prove inline from the loop laws that conjugation by this path is a basepoint-change isomorphism; this transfers triviality to every basepoint. The same radial paths and sphere paths prove path-connectedness. State the n=2 and n≥3 clauses separately and do not claim anything at n=0 or n=1.

items.title: $\mathbb R^2$ is not homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$ for $n\ne2$
items.strategy: Treat every natural n. For n=0, R^0 is a singleton while R^2 has distinct points. For n=1, use the published theorem that R is not homeomorphic to any higher-dimensional Euclidean space and symmetry of homeomorphism. For n≥3, suppose h:R^2→R^n is a homeomorphism. Translate so h(0)=0 and postcompose with an explicit invertible coordinate shear and permutation carrying h(e_0) to e_0. Restriction then gives a pointed homeomorphism of punctured spaces, hence an isomorphism of their fundamental groups, contradicting the preceding Z-versus-trivial calculation. Write the coordinate homeomorphism and its inverse, including the choice of a nonzero coordinate.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring is compact and path-connected
items.strategy: For n≥1 let C_n be the circle of radius 1/n centred at (1/n,0), and let H be their union. The union is bounded. To prove it closed, note that all sufficiently small circles lie in any prescribed ball about the origin, while away from the origin only finitely many circles remain relevant; a point outside their finite closed union has a disjoint neighbourhood. Heine–Borel gives compactness. Every point lies on one C_n and can be joined within that circle to the common origin, so concatenating two such paths gives path-connectedness. Keep the index n≥1 explicit so no radius 1/0 occurs.

title: Applications of the Fundamental Group — Examples

items.title: Radial normalization retracts the punctured disk, but it cannot extend to the disk
items.strategy: Restrict x↦x/|x| to D^2∖{0}; the published radial deformation retraction shows it continuously retracts that punctured disk onto S^1. Any continuous extension agreeing on S^1 would be a retraction D^2→S^1, forbidden by the no-retraction theorem. Show directly that approaching zero along two different rays gives different limiting values.

items.title: The large-circle loop of $z^3-2z+2$ on $|z|=5$ has degree three
items.strategy: The lower-coefficient modulus sum is 4<5. Apply the large-radius polynomial-loop lemma to p(z)=z^3-2z+2 and R=5, and display the coefficient-scaling homotopy to the threefold standard loop. Verify directly that the leading-term bound is strict throughout.

items.title: Orthogonal projection $S^2\to\mathbb R^2$ has exactly one antipodal pair with equal image
items.strategy: For q(x,y,z)=(x,y), equality q(v)=q(-v) forces x=y=0. Unit norm then leaves precisely the north-south antipodal pair. Verify continuity componentwise and distinguish one antipodal pair from two points.

items.title: Four closed sets can cover $S^2$ without any one containing an antipodal pair
items.strategy: Take the four Voronoi regions determined by the vertices of a regular tetrahedron centred at the origin: A_i consists of sphere points whose inner product with v_i is maximal. Finite intersections of closed half-spaces make the regions closed, and a finite maximum makes them cover. If x and -x both lay in A_i, every inner product with x would tie; the three differences v_i-v_j span R^3, forcing x=0, impossible on S^2. Give explicit tetrahedral vertices and verify the spanning calculation.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring retracts onto each of its circles
items.strategy: For fixed n, define r_n to be the identity on C_n and send every other circle to the common origin. Away from the origin, a relative neighbourhood meets only the relevant branch and continuity is immediate. At the origin, preimages of neighbourhoods in C_n contain a sufficiently small planar neighbourhood intersected with the earring; equivalently verify continuity by the subspace closed-set criterion. Thus r_n is continuous and restricts to the identity on C_n.

items.title: FALSE: every compact path-connected subset of $\mathbb R^2$ has a universal cover
items.strategy: Use the Hawaiian earring. The A-page proposition gives compactness and path-connectedness. Every neighbourhood of the origin contains C_n for all sufficiently large n. The preceding retraction r_n makes the inclusion of C_n injective on fundamental groups, so its standard loop remains essential in the earring. Hence no neighbourhood kills all loop classes, semilocal simple connectedness fails, and the universal-cover necessity theorem rules out a universal cover.
